title: GDPR security: could you prove your measures fit the risk?
short: Require MFA on every remote login, link each processing record to its systems and keep dated proof that you test your measures.
answer: This quarter, require MFA on every remote, partner and admin login, and link each entry in your Article 30 records to the systems, processors and measures that protect it. Judge every other measure by the harm a breach would do to the people concerned and by what the state of the art offers, because in a damages claim you must prove your measures were appropriate[^c340].
audience: IT, security and data protection teams in companies in Germany and the EU

blocks.title: If you only do five things

items.title: Require MFA for every remote, partner and admin login.
items.text: Nearly 80% of the large breaches the CNIL saw in 2024 used an account protected only by a password, and from 2026 it checks large databases for MFA[^cnilbdd]. See the passkeys-mfa sheet.

items.title: Link your records of processing to your asset list.
items.text: Give every Article 30 entry the systems and processors it uses and a general description of their security measures[^gdpr], so no system goes live without an owner and a risk rating.

items.title: Make processor contracts specific.
items.text: Attach a concrete security annex[^scc] that requires your approval for changes and a regular review[^edpb0720].

items.title: Patch known flaws and watch for bulk data access.
items.text: Patch within the patching sheet's deadlines. For large databases the CNIL expects alerts and caps on bulk exports[^cnilbdd].

items.title: Clear monitoring tools with the works council first.
items.text: The works council co-determines any system that records individualizable behavior or performance data, whatever you intend[^bag]. DLP that profiles staff also needs a DPIA[^dskmuss].

blocks.title: Show that your measures fit the risk

items.title: Which systems process the data?
items.text: Start from the Article 30 record. SDM 3.1 asks you to show that each means of processing, especially technical ones, is used lawfully[^sdmmv].

items.title: How much harm could a breach do?
items.text: Rate the risk for the people concerned, not for the company. Where your IT-Grundschutz rating differs, the SDM suggests the measures for the higher one[^sdm]. Likely high risk needs a DPIA first[^gdpr].

items.title: What does the state of the art offer?
items.text: A moving target: what the market offers, as recognized standards show. Cost can shape the choice of measure but is no reason to skip one[^edpb25].

items.title: Do the measures work?
items.text: Article 32 requires a process for regular testing and evaluation[^gdpr]. Schedule restore tests, access reviews and exposure scans, and keep the results.

items.title: Could you prove it in court?
items.text: A breach alone doesn't show your measures were inappropriate, but in a damages claim the burden of proof is yours[^c340].

blocks.title: What authorities fined for, 2024 to 2026
items: **Weak remote logins.** The CNIL fined Free Mobile and Free €42 million in January 2026 for weak VPN logins and failed detection of abnormal activity[^cnilfree]. A private hospital paid €500,000 in September 2026: external doctors reached records without VPN or MFA, and the attacker browsed for days unnoticed[^cnilhpl].

**Accounts that see too much.** France Travail's €5 million fine in January 2026 cited weak authentication, too little logging and partner advisers who could see jobseekers they didn't support[^cnilft].

**Weak identity checks, unmonitored partners.** The BfDI fined Vodafone €45 million in June 2025: €30 million for portal and hotline authentication flaws that exposed eSIM profiles, €15 million for not monitoring partner agencies[^bfdi].
**Known flaws left open.** Italy's Garante fined Postel €900,000 in October 2024 for a flaw left unpatched for almost a year after the vendor and the national cyber agency flagged it[^postel].
**No log review, no MFA.** IQVIA's €5 million fine in May 2026 covered unreviewed connection logs and no MFA on a health data warehouse[^cniliqvia].

**Secrets and design.** The Irish DPC fined Meta €91 million in 2024 for plaintext passwords[^dpc91] and €251 million, €240 million of it under Article 25, for a flaw that exposed access tokens[^dpc251].

blocks.title: Processor contracts and the security annex
items: **Describe measures concretely.** The standard clauses rule out generic descriptions[^scc]; the EDPB wants enough detail for you to judge them[^edpb0720].

**Know every subprocessor.** Keep each one's name, address and contact at hand; the processor should supply and update them[^op22]. Under a general authorization, you get notice of changes and a chance to object[^gdpr].

**Scale checks to the risk.** Verify every processor, more deeply where the risk is higher[^op22]. For databases of millions of people, the CNIL expects the security policy and certificates annexed and periodic audits[^cnilbdd].
**Use the other sheets** for supplier tiers and exit terms (third-party-risk) and for AI providers (ai-input-security).

blocks.title: Security monitoring and staff
items: **Don't rely on § 26 BDSG alone.** The CJEU found a clause worded like § 26(1) appears merely to restate the GDPR; clauses that fail Article 88(2) must be disregarded[^c34]. Document an Article 6 basis per tool.

**Agree each tool with the works council.** It co-determines systems that record individualizable behavior or performance data, with no threshold for minor tools[^bag]. Courts fully review whether a works agreement's processing is necessary[^c65].

**Write a logging concept.** Per processing activity, state what is logged, where, why, who may read it and when it is deleted[^b43]; the CNIL suggests six months to a year for access logs[^cnilbdd]. Logs kept to check admin work must not be used to rate their speed[^b43].

blocks.title: How German authorities judge measures
items: **The SDM is the yardstick.** It maps GDPR duties to seven goals[^sdm], and the DSK recommends it with its catalog of reference measures[^sdmmv].

**Email needs enforced TLS.** For high risk, the DSK expects end-to-end plus qualified transport encryption: TR-02102-2 ciphers, forward secrecy and DNSSEC-checked servers. Professional secrecy indicates high risk[^dskmail].
**The DPIA must-list** names DLP that profiles staff, employee geolocation and AI that evaluates people or steers interaction with them[^dskmuss].

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **The SDM logging module was rewritten.** Building block 43 v2.0, valid since 1 June 2026, asks for an organization-wide logging concept[^b43].
**Fixed procedures for cross-border cases.** From 2 April 2027, lead authorities must send preliminary findings and allow three to six weeks to reply[^proc].

**Fewer firms may need records.** The agreed Omnibus IV text exempts organizations under 1,000 staff except for high-risk processing[^st10482]; Parliament is due to vote on 23 November 2026[^oeil130].
**The Digital Omnibus is pending.** Its GDPR changes await a committee decision in Parliament[^oeil360].

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **End-to-end encryption for all email.** The DSK requires it only for high risk[^dskmail]. Enforce TLS for the rest.
**A certificate to prove Article 32.** Approved certifications and codes of conduct are only one element of proof[^gdpr]. Spend on the controls.
**Collecting every subprocessor contract.** The EDPB says you needn't ask for them systematically[^op22].
**A DPIA for every system.** The Article 29 Working Party expects one mainly where two of its nine criteria apply[^wp248]. File a screening note for the rest.

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Naming measures and not building them.** The CNIL held it against France Travail that its DPIAs listed most of the missing measures[^cnilft].
**Leaving processors out of scope.** A significant share of the large breaches the CNIL saw in 2024 involved a processor with weak security[^cnilbdd].
**Ignoring small claims.** The BGH held that a mere loss of control can be damage and accepted about €100 per person[^bgh]. Across a large breach, that adds up.
**Dropping records under Omnibus IV.** High-risk processing would still need them[^st10482], and without them you can't scope a breach.

blocks.title: What this looks like at your size

columns.title: Small team, no security staff
items: Keep records even with fewer than 250 staff: the exemption doesn't cover processing that isn't occasional, such as payroll[^gdpr].
Turn on MFA for email, VPN and remote support tools first.
File each provider's standard processing agreement with its security annex and subprocessor list.

columns.title: Growing, with IT or security staff
items: Make the Article 30 entry, risk rating and owner required fields when a system enters the asset list.
Sign one framework works agreement for security tools that sets purposes, data, access, retention and the procedure on suspicion[^bfdifaq].
Keep a yearly test plan and its results as Article 32 evidence.

columns.title: Enterprise or regulated
items: Map SDM goals to your ISMS controls so one evidence set serves the GDPR, NIS2 and ISO 27001 (see the isms and eu-security-laws sheets).
Audit high-risk processors and the subprocessors behind them on a schedule.
Name who answers preliminary findings, which may allow only three weeks from April 2027[^proc].

changes.text: First draft, based on the GDPR, CJEU judgments C-340/21, C-34/21 and C-65/23, DSK and EDPB guidance, and 2024 to 2026 fines by the CNIL, BfDI, DPC and Garante.
